history.alt_text: Unbranded smartphone battery beside a mechanical cycle counter on a weathered concrete workbench
history.caption: The battery's published cycle count, embodied by a mechanical counter with a reset lever, frames the swap as a consumable parts decision.
history.title: Battery Cycle Counter on Workbench

style_when: the news is structural and abstract — a stack reordered, a layer added, a flow rerouted — and there is no literal object that carries it, so the idea is stated as a small physical assembly of recognisable parts rather than as bare shapes
prompt: A matte clay 3D render of a flat rectangular unbranded smartphone battery with rounded corners, two gold contact pads, and a thin ribbon cable, resting on a weathered concrete workbench at the left third. Beside it on the right stands a mechanical cycle counter module: a cylindrical tally drum with notched ridges and a small latching reset lever, mounted on a brushed steel bracket. One directional key light from the left rakes across the matte surfaces, throwing long contact shadows to the right. Palette: bone white, graphite, olive. Asymmetric off-centre composition with generous negative space. No text, no logos, no digits.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, watermarks, illegible text, blurry text, embossed text, printed numbers, digits, UI elements
rationale: The story turns on a numerical rating (cycle count) governing a physical part's lifespan; a matte clay render can construct the battery and counting mechanism as a tangible assembly without relying on legible text, avoiding the previous rejection's illegible lettering and ambiguous power-bank look.
cue: the swap that resets the counter
subject: an unbranded smartphone battery beside a mechanical cycle counter with a reset lever
core_thesis: A phone battery's service life is published as a full-charge-cycle count—500 for older iPhones, 1000 from the 15, and 800 as the EU minimum—making the battery a $47-$99 parts decision, not a handset replacement.
core_conflict: Published cycle-count ratings (500/1000/800) collide with real-world capacity fade and warranty timing, forcing owners to weigh a cheap battery swap against replacing an otherwise functional handset.
composition: asymmetric off-centre composition with the battery at the left third and the counter at the right, generous negative space, 16:9
alt_text: Your Battery Dies At 500 Cycles. Unbranded smartphone battery beside a mechanical cycle counter on a weathered concrete workbench
caption: Your Battery Dies At 500 Cycles: A phone battery dies on a published cycle count, not a calendar date.
title: Your Battery Dies At 500 Cycles
